title: Non-invasive chimeric HaloTag labeling to study clustering and diffusion of membrane proteins
protocol: Streak out bacteria from the glycerol stock in the -80°C freezer onto an LB plate (with no antibiotics) and grow for 12–18 hours at 37°C.
Inoculate a single colony into 5 ml of LB liquid medium and shake at 37°C for 12-18 hours.
Store the bacterial culture at 4°C for up to 3 months.
Prepare S medium by mixing ingredients listed in the Key Resource Table.
Prepare egg buffer by mixing ingredients listed in the Key Resource Table.
Prepare two 1.5 mL tubes, label as JF585 and JF646.
Add 1 mL of HB101 liquid culture in each tube.
Spin down the bacteria by centrifuge at 1500 x g for 3 min.
Remove the supernatant.
Add 100 μL S media to each tube, resuspend by pipetting up and down.
Dissolve one aliquot of JF585 and one aliquot of JF646 in 2 μL DMSO to reconstitute a 1 mM stock.
Add 1.5 μL of dissolved JF585 to the respective tube of bacterial suspension.
Add 1.5 μL of dissolved JF646 to the respective tube of bacterial suspension.
Mix each bacterial suspension with the respective fluorescent dye to achieve a final concentration of 15 μM.
Add 2 μL of JF585-medium-bacteria mix to 100 μL JF646-medium-bacteria mix to obtain a 1:50 ratio of JF585:JF646 in the final culture.
Transfer 30 μL of the dye mixture to one well of a round-bottom 96-well plate.
Pick 20–30 L4 worms into the culture containing the dye mixture.
Add approximately 200 μL of water to adjacent wells or seal with parafilm to prevent drying out.
Shake at 225 rpm in a 20°C incubator for 16-18 hours.
Turn on the microscope and configure acquisition before preparing the sample.
Dilute TetraSpeck fluorescent glass beads 1:50 in water.
Plasma treat a glass coverslip for 3–5 min on maximum power.
Soak a glass coverslip in 1 M KOH for 20–30 min and then rinse with plenty of water if plasma cleaner is not available.
Vortex the TetraSpeck beads vigorously.
Transfer 15–20 μl beads to the prepared coverslip.
Place the coverslip on a cold hot plate, turn on, and leave until liquid evaporates (20–30 s).
Add 10 μL of egg buffer, PBS or water.
Using a dry pipette tip, add a small amount of glass spacer beads by dipping the pipette tip into the vial and touching it to the liquid droplet.
Cover with a microscope slide and seal with VALAP.
View live images of the beads with the red and far-red channels overlaid on the dual-view microscope.
Adjust the laser power to 5 mW at 561 nm for sufficient visualization.
Align the image splitter so that the two channels are perfectly aligned.
Acquire a reference image of the beads.
Excite the desired sample with a 561 nm laser.
Gradually increase the laser power until single molecules can be visualized clearly by eye in live images.
Lower the laser power if phototoxicity is observed.
Set exposure time to 50 ms.
Set imaging frequency to 20 frames per second.
Dissect worms to obtain embryos.
Add 11 μL droplet of polylysine on a microscope slide.
Place a 22 mm × 22 mm coverslip on top of the droplet.
Bake on hot plate at >100°C for ∼30 s until all liquid evaporates.
Take 1 worm out of the 96-well plate using a hook-shaped worm pick.
Check the stage; worms should be young adults with a single row of 8–10 eggs.
Use a glass pipette to transfer the whole 30 μL liquid culture onto an OP50 NGM plate.
Let the liquid dry out and let the worms crawl on the plate for at least 30 minutes before imaging.
Add 30 μL of egg buffer into a watch glass slide.
Transfer 2–3 labeled worms from the NGM plate to the watch glass slide.
Cut each worm in half with a pair of 26-gauge needles to release the embryos.
Mount the embryos. Place the coverslip on a clean surface, polylysine-coated side up.
Add a 10 μL droplet of egg buffer onto the coverslip.
Using a dry pipette tip, add a small amount of 23–26 mm glass spacer beads to the liquid droplet.
Transfer an embryo of the desired stage onto the coverslip using a glass micro needle.
Gently place a microscope slide on top of the coverslip containing the embryo.
Seal with VALAP.
Locate the embryo under the microscope.
Draw a cross mark on the slide to mark the position of each embryo.
Place the slide on the microscope stage.
Move the objective lens to the upper left quadrant of the cross.
View live images using brightfield illumination.
Turn off any autoscaling function in the imaging software.
Move the stage towards the right slowly until the image darkens, corresponding to the shadow of the cross mark.
Move the imaging field down while scanning left and right until the embryo is located.
Focus at the lower cortex of the embryo.
Turn off the brightfield channel.
Switch to the far red (abundant dye) channel.
Take snapshots while adjusting the focus until fluorescent foci are in focus.
Adjust the penetration depth until cortical proteins are clearly visualized.
Ensure the background signal is as low as possible.
Acquire timelapse images using the red+far red dualview imaging channel as configured in “Microscope settings.”
Perform particle tracking with Utrack for particle diffusion analysis.
Examine the tracking results to ensure accurate detection and linking of particles.
Correctly detect particles, ensuring dimmer foci are not missed.
Link detected particles accurately, connecting gaps without creating long straight lines or sharp turns.
Download and install ImageJ.
Download and install MATLAB.
Download Utrack from https://github.com/DanuserLab/u-track.
Add Utrack to the MATLAB file folder, where all other scripts are stored.
Launch MATLAB, locate ‘u-track-master’ in the file navigator, right click ->‘Add to Path’ -> ‘Selected Folders and Subfolders’.
Download the ‘DualLabeling_Analysis’ package from https://github.com/dickinson-lab/DualLabeling_Analysis.
Add to MATLAB file folder and ‘add to path’.
Use ImageJ to split the channels in the movie into two different movies.
Use the 'Save -> Image Sequence' command to export each channel to an image sequence in its own separate folder.
Track sparsely labeled particles with Utrack.
Launch Utrack using the MATLAB command movieSelectorGUI.
Click ‘New’ to open a new window for ‘Movie edition’.
In the ‘Channels’ section, click ‘Add Channel’, then select the folder containing the image sequence of sparse/JF585 channel.
Enter the requested information in the ‘Advanced Channel Settings’ and ‘Movie Information’ sections.
Select your ‘Output Path’ where data will be saved.
Click ‘Continue’ in the ‘Movie selection’ window to proceed with particle tracking.
Select ‘[2D] Single particles’ from the options, then click ‘OK’.
Check 'Step 1: Detection' and click on 'Settings'.
Select 'point source detection' and click 'Settings…'.
In the new window, set 'Alpha' to 0.03 in the 'Parameters for' section.
Click 'Apply'.
Check 'Step 2: Tracking' and click on 'Settings'.
A new window will appear.
In the 'Parameters' section, set 'Maximum Gap to Close' to 3.
Set 'Minimum Length of Track Segments from First Step' to 2.
Click on 'Apply'.
Adjust the maximum GAP according to particle density.
Decrease the value of Alpha if background noise is falsely detected as particles.
Increase the value of Alpha if some real particles are missed.
Check and uncheck ‘point sources’ in the ‘Viewer’ window while looking at the ‘Movie’ window.
Click ‘Results’ for step 1.
4 windows will appear after clicking 'Run'.
Click ‘Results’ for step 2.
Check 'Static tracks' in the 'Viewer' window.
Examine track appearance in the 'Movie' window.
Reduce the ‘Maximum Gap to Close’ if outstanding long straight lines or sharp angles are observed.
Locate the results file Output path -> TrackingPackage -> tracks -> Channel_1_tracking_result.mat in your output data folder.
Drag the results file into MATLAB workspace.
Use command tracks = convert_Utrack(tracksFinal) to organize 'tracksFinal' into a more readable format.
Download ‘MSDanalyzer’ from https://tinevez.github.io/msdanalyzer/.
Add downloaded software to MATLAB file folder and 'add to path'.
Install ‘SLM toolbox’ from https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/24443-slm-shape-language-modeling.
Launch MATLAB if not already running.
Re-organize Utrack result by using the command tracks = convert_Utrack(tracksFinal).
Generate linear MSD plots and transform to log-log scale using msd = runMSD(tracks), followed by set(gca, 'YScale', 'log').
Set gca XScale to 'log'.
Remove tracks shorter than 0.5 s to reduce background noise and cytoplasmic PAR-3 signal.
Use PickLongTracks script with a minimum of 10 frames per track for analysis inclusion.
Inspect plots to identify particle motion type.
A straight line on the linear-scale plot indicates normal diffusion.
Concave-up or concave-down curves indicate directed or confined motion, respectively.
Straight lines on the log-log plot indicate time-invariant motion with a slope indicating the type of motion.
MSD curves not straight on a log-log plot indicate different kinds of motion on different timescales.
Engineered hexameric PAR-3 exhibits confined diffusion on short timescales but directed motion on longer timescales.
Estimate the diffusion coefficient.
Determine the diffusion coefficient of a membrane-bound species by fitting linear-scale MSD curves to the 2D diffusion equation: MSD = 4Dtα.
Fit the curve using the curve fitting toolbox within MATLAB or ezyfit.
For cases with different kinds of motion on different timescales, fit only the first few time steps of the MSD curve when the motion is close to normal diffusion.
Estimate the anomalous parameter α from the fit obtained in step 21a for time-invariant diffusion cases.
Visualize the anomalous parameter at different time lags by estimating the derivative of the log-log MSD plot for non-time-invariant situations.
Check that the ‘msd’ variable is defined in the MATLAB workspace.
Run step 20a again if the ‘msd’ variable is not defined.
Extract the log mean MSD curve using the command logMeanMSD = log10(msd.getMeanMSD).
Visualize different values of the anomalous parameter on different timescales.
Estimate the slope of the log-log MSD curve by taking the first derivative of a spline fit to the data.
Run the following command: slm = slmengine(logMeanMSD(:, 1), logMeanMSD(:, 2), 'plot', 'on').
Plot the first derivative from the “Plot” menu in the figure window.
Extract the first derivative to a vector for further analysis using: alpha = slmeval(logMeanMSD(:, 1), slm, 1).
Constrain the fit to only shorter timescales where data are not too noisy by limiting the range of values passed to slmengine.
For example, plot and fit only the first 100 time delays using: slm = slmengine(logMeanMSD(1:100, 1), logMeanMSD(1:100, 2), 'plot', 'on').
Prepare 3 microcentrifuge tubes as described above.
Transfer 2 μL of tube 1 mix into tube 3.
Transfer 1 μL of tube 2 mix into tube 3.
Feed worm as described in the ‘preparing C. elegans for HaloTag imaging’ section.
Acquire movies as described in the ‘dissecting, mounting and imaging’ section.
Repeat the process for 3 embryos.
Extract intensity information from the calibration experiment for both channels.
Save the first frame of each channel as a single-plane TIFF file.
Feed the first frame of each into Utrack as described above.
Run the ‘detection’ step only in Utrack.
Reorganize the results using the “convert_Utrack” script.
Copy all [amp] intensity datasets for all repeats in both channels into an Excel spreadsheet.
Calculate the cluster size of far-red clusters.
Determine the ratio of average single far-red dye intensity to the average single red dye intensity.
Convert each intensity dataset to log scale.
Plot individual values in Graphpad Prism or another graphing software.
Calculate the mean (log) intensity for each channel and each embryo.
Normalize each red channel mean intensity to 1 by dividing the red intensity by the red channel average from the same movie.
Normalize the corresponding far-red channel average from the same embryo by dividing the farred intensity by the red channel average.
Pool all replicate datasets together.
Calculate the ratio of the average single far-red dye intensity to the average single red dye intensity.
Extract the intensity information of red dyes in each sparse/abundant dual-labeling experiment.
Determine the farred channel intensity for each corresponding farred foci using a specific script.
Convert each intensity dataset to log scale.
Calculate the mean (log) intensity for each dataset.
Normalize all red channel averages to 1 by dividing the red intensity by the red channel average from the same movie.
Correct the corresponding far-red cluster intensity in log space.
Convert calibrated far-red cluster intensities back to normal scale using: Calibrated absolute farred cluster intensity = e^(calibrated log farred cluster intensity).
Calculate the cluster size using: Farred cluster size = calibrated absolute farred cluster intensity / e.
